Neonates of the luminous bay squid emerge from the egg capsule with a mantle length of only 0.28 cm [Lb = 0.28 cm], a diminutive size that underscores the substantial energetic investment required to reach the juvenile stage. Hatchlings possess a fully functional gladius and a well-developed ink sac, which are immediately deployed for propulsion and predator evasion in the shallow, productive waters of their continental shelf habitat. Field surveys conducted in the subtropical waters of eastern Australia indicate that this birth size is consistent with values reported for other myopsid squids of comparable egg diameter. The minute paralarvae are initially planktonic and feed on copepod nauplii and microzooplankton, relying on their rudimentary fins and mantle jet for vertical movement within the water column. Growth is rapid during the first weeks of exogenous feeding, a trait common to many coastal loliginids.

At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the complete life cycle of Uroteuthis noctiluca encompasses a maximum lifespan of 250.0 d [am = 250.0 d], which classifies this species as a short-lived, semelparous cephalopod typical of tropical and subtropical inshore assemblages. This relatively compressed lifespan likely reflects the high metabolic costs associated with its active, predatory lifestyle, as well as the elevated predation pressure it faces from larger fish and marine mammals. Comparative data from congeneric species show that lifespan in the Loliginidae is inversely correlated with habitat temperature, a pattern that is recapitulated here under controlled experimental conditions. Individuals held in mesocosm tanks at this stable temperature display a consistent mortality schedule, with senescence becoming evident after approximately seven months of age.

Puberty in this species is attained once females reach a mantle length of 2.6 cm [Lp = 2.6 cm], a developmental milestone that typically occurs before the animal has completed its somatic growth. Histological examination of the reproductive tract reveals that the onset of vitellogenesis coincides with this mantle length, marking the transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive investment. This size at maturity is relatively low compared to that of the closely related Uroteuthis edulis, in which females mature at slightly larger dimensions, but is consistent with the pace of life seen in other small, warm-water loliginids. At the point of senescence, the squid attains a maximum mantle length of 9.0 cm [Li = 9.0 cm], representing a roughly 30-fold increase in linear dimensions since hatching.

By the end of its life, the average female luminous bay squid deposits a cumulative total of 1788.0 eggs , a figure determined under the standard thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] used throughout the experimental trials. This total reproductive output is the result of multiple sequential spawning events, each batching a portion of the ovarian egg complement over the final weeks of the lifespan. The egg mass is deposited in gelatinous strands that are anchored to seagrass blades or rocky substrates, providing mechanical protection for the developing embryos. The number of oocytes spawned per individual is correlated with female size at death, with larger females typically delivering a greater fecundity. This value of approximately 1800 eggs per lifetime is comparable to fecundities reported for other neritic loliginids of similar adult body proportions.

The wet weight recorded at the time of death for a typical individual reared under laboratory conditions is 15.26 g [Wwi = 15.26 g], a body mass that reflects the packing of both somatic and reproductive tissues accumulated over the growing season. This weight represents the maximum post-spawning mass, as the female has already deposited her egg complement by the time of natural mortality. In field-caught specimens from the same geographic region, terminal wet weights range slightly above and below this value depending on local prey availability and water temperature. The somatic mass fraction at death is considerably higher than the birth mass, illustrating the extensive tissue accretion that occurs during the relatively brief juvenile and subadult growth phases. This mass at death is consistent with an allometric scaling relationship derived from adult mantle length data in the congener Uroteuthis edulis.
